prose: SELL. The 12-month target price is USD 135.0, implying 58.9% downside from the current price of USD 328.58.

The current price requires economics far beyond the followed model’s 2026 forecast of USD 93.9 billion revenue and USD 6.9 billion EBIT. The reverse valuation reaches the market capitalization only if 2027 EBIT rises to USD 55.5 billion on virtually unchanged revenue, implying a 59.4% EBIT margin. This is inconsistent with Tesla’s Q2 automotive gross margin of 16.3% excluding credits and the model’s 2026 group EBIT margin of 7.4%, unless high-margin autonomy and software dominate unusually quickly.

The evidence is not uniformly bearish. Tesla delivered a record 480,126 vehicles in Q2 2026, had 1.48 million active FSD subscribers, operated robotaxi services in seven US metropolitan areas and generated attractive energy-segment gross profit. It also has a cost advantage if a roughly USD 400 vision-only sensor suite can safely perform work that costs far more with multi-sensor systems. These assets justify option value well above conventional automotive peers.

The strongest challenge to the SELL call is that a scalable driverless network could address nearly USD 10 trillion of annual transportation activity, rather than the much smaller current robotaxi market. If Tesla proves rider-only safety, secures driverless permissions beyond Texas, and approaches its USD 0.20-per-mile cost target, the network could create more value than automotive. The report still assigns a majority failure outcome because California permits Tesla only with a driver and disclosed driverless evidence remains well behind Waymo.

The call would improve to HOLD or BUY if independently auditable driverless miles, intervention frequency and contribution margin support a nationwide rollout, or if Optimus demonstrates repeatable multi-task work at a commercially competitive cost. It would become more negative if automotive margin remains near the mid-teens while capital expenditure exceeds USD 25 billion, energy gross profitability reverses, or FSD attachment and retention stop rising.

The USD 161.7 target explicitly values the operating businesses and autonomy options rather than extrapolating the share-price move.

valuePools.name: Automotive manufacturing and leasing
deepDive: ### The prize is global vehicle and ownership expenditure

Tesla competes in a USD 4.36 trillion global automotive market for 2025, estimated by Market Research Future in August 2026. The relevant economic pool is broader than annual vehicle sales. Vehicle ownership absorbs approximately 17% of household expenses, according to The Zebra’s August 2026 assessment, including purchase, depreciation, financing, insurance, maintenance and energy. Tesla currently captures manufacturing revenue, leasing income, regulatory credits and related service activity, not the full ownership wallet. The valuation therefore uses achievable vehicle revenue and margin rather than a direct share of this multi-trillion-dollar pool. At USD 76.8 billion of modelled FY2025 division revenue, Tesla captures less than 2% of the labeled global automotive market. Market size is not the immediate constraint; gross margin at the delivery volumes needed to use installed factories is.
### The required share is plausible, but the margin is not yet secure

A USD 240.0 billion enterprise value for this division is supported by the report’s target-year EBITDA estimate of USD 24.0 billion at 10.0x. At a mature 14% automotive EBITDA margin, this requires approximately USD 171 billion of revenue. At USD 43,000 per delivered vehicle, that implies about 4.0 million annual vehicle-equivalents before leasing, credits and service revenue. This is demanding but not implausible in a USD 4.36 trillion market, representing approximately 3.9% by revenue. The harder task is doubling volume while preserving pricing and restoring margin. Q2 2026 automotive revenue per delivered vehicle had fallen below USD 43,000 from more than USD 50,000 in 2021. Tesla must combine lower unit cost, better capacity utilization and less discounting. The base valuation excludes autonomy revenue from vehicle EBITDA; that value is assigned separately to paid software and robotaxi.
### Reported and modelled boundaries must remain separate

Tesla’s verified FY2025 Automotive segment control is USD 82.1 billion of external sales and USD 13.3 billion of gross profit, or 86.5% of group revenue and 77.8% of group gross profit. This reported segment includes activities assigned elsewhere in the report, notably charging and software, so it is not the automotive-manufacturing division. The report models manufacturing and leasing revenue at USD 76.8 billion by starting with USD 94.8 billion of group revenue, then subtracting USD 12.8 billion of energy revenue, USD 3.6 billion of estimated paid charging revenue and USD 1.6 billion of modelled paid-software revenue. The resulting boundary includes vehicle sales, USD 2 billion of regulatory-credit revenue, USD 1.7 billion of leasing revenue and residual automotive services. Gross profit is also allocated rather than reported: USD 11.3 billion after assigning USD 1.2 billion to software and USD 720 million to paid charging. This preserves demonstrable revenue while recognizing that Tesla does not report these business divisions.
### Demand has recovered, but global leadership is contested

- Tesla delivered 480,126 vehicles in Q2 2026, up 25% year over year and a quarterly record.
- BYD sold 557,090 BEVs in Q2 2026, above Tesla’s 480,126, and regained the quarterly global lead.
- Tesla retained 50.5% of US EV sales in Q2 2026, while its first-quarter global BEV share was estimated at approximately 13%.
- BYD delivered 2,256,714 all-electric vehicles in 2025. Another source rounded this to 2.26 million, so the difference is rounding rather than a different conclusion.

The evidence supports a strong US franchise, not unchallenged global leadership. Cox Automotive measured Tesla at 50.5% of US EV sales in Q2, while EVwire reported a 52.3% first-half share; the periods are compatible. In China, BYD held 23.5% of the broader NEV retail market in July 2026. In Europe, BEVs represented 19.7% of new-car registrations during the first four months, leaving room for Volkswagen and other local producers. Scale improves procurement, factory absorption and pricing flexibility, but competition means capacity expansion alone is insufficient. Tesla’s 10 millionth vehicle and Shanghai’s six millionth battery pack show industrial learning. They do not prove that future incremental vehicles will earn the margin in the base valuation.
### Factory utilization is the operating fulcrum

Shanghai has approximately one million vehicles of annual capacity and is Tesla’s largest, most utilized plant. Berlin produced 61,000 Model Ys in Q1 2026 and operated at approximately 65% of its 375,000-unit annual installed capacity. That implies roughly 131,000 units of unused annualized capacity at Berlin, calculated as 35% of 375,000, although quarterly mix and downtime make this approximate. Specific 2026 utilization for Texas and Fremont is unavailable, preventing a reliable group calculation. Tesla’s Q2 update says it decommissioned Model S and X lines at Fremont to build Optimus capacity. Saying the models were discontinued is directionally correct but less precise because the official statement identifies a production-line conversion and capital reallocation. Fewer low-volume configurations may simplify automotive production, but the move reduces premium-price breadth and redirects capital from current vehicles to an unproven option.
### Margin evidence remains below the level needed for a premium valuation

Two Q2 sources differ because they use different definitions. MLQ.ai reported a 16.3% automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits, while Statista reported a 16.7% automotive gross margin. The report uses 16.3% because excluding credits better reflects vehicle economics and credits fell 67% year over year to USD 146 million. BYD’s FY2025 automotive gross margin was 20.5%, above Tesla’s 17.8%, while Toyota’s group gross margin was 16.7% for the fiscal year to March 2026. Volkswagen’s 3.8% first-half operating return shows that gross margin does not translate directly into EBIT after selling, engineering and corporate costs. Tesla’s 2025 group EBIT margin was 4.6%, and the followed model reaches 7.4% in 2026. A 14% division EBITDA margin at scale assumes meaningful cost absorption and mix recovery, while remaining below software economics.
### Leasing adds resilience, but disclosed margin evidence is limited

FY2025 automotive leasing revenue was USD 1.7 billion. Q2 2026 leasing revenue fell to USD 364 million from USD 435 million one year earlier. Leasing can support residual values, improve control of used inventory and smooth affordability, but it retains asset and resale-price risk. Tesla remains small versus specialist fleet managers: Ayvens operated approximately 3.1 million vehicles in August 2026 and Arval financed nearly 1.9 million vehicles at the end of 2025. Europe represented an estimated 39.2% of global automotive leasing and finance revenue in 2025, making local residual values and financing terms important to expansion. Tesla does not disclose leasing gross margin, so the valuation gives leasing no premium multiple. Lower used-car prices would hurt lease economics and new-vehicle affordability through trade-in values.
### Capital intensity limits the value of growth without cash conversion

Tesla’s 2025 FCFF was negative USD 383 million after USD 11.2 billion of gross capital expenditure. The followed model expects USD 3.5 billion of FCFF in 2026 on USD 8.3 billion of capex. External reporting after Q2 indicated full-year capex could exceed USD 25 billion, while Q2 alone reached USD 5.8 billion. This is a material forecast-timing risk, not a minor variance. If capex exceeds USD 25 billion while operating profit remains near the followed model, annual cash generation will be materially lower. Some investment supports robotaxi, batteries and robotics rather than automotive, but shareholders fund it from the same balance sheet. The base automotive multiple is therefore 10.0x target-year EBITDA, below Tesla’s normalized 101.83x historical group EV/EBITDA and closer to established mobility and manufacturing levels than to its share-price history.
### What would validate or break the automotive value

Validation requires annualized deliveries to approach four million units, automotive gross margin excluding credits to recover above 20%, revenue per vehicle to stabilize, and capex to produce higher utilized capacity. Strong near-term evidence would include sustained delivery records without price cuts, Berlin utilization above its reported 65%, and group free cash flow despite AI investment. The value breaks if Tesla needs continued discounting to fill factories, if BYD sustains higher gross margin while growing faster, or if regulatory credits keep falling before manufacturing costs catch up. At a 10% rather than 14% EBITDA margin, the same USD 24 billion of EBITDA requires USD 240 billion of revenue, or about 5.6 million vehicles at USD 43,000 each. Holding USD 171 billion of revenue at a 10% margin would reduce EBITDA to USD 17.1 billion and value to roughly USD 171 billion at 10.0x, USD 69 billion below the base automotive value. Sustainable gross margin, not headline delivery growth, is therefore decisive.

valuePools.name: Unsupervised autonomy and robotaxi network
deepDive: ### The prize is transportation spending, not today’s robotaxi market

The global transportation-services market could reach approximately USD 9.98 trillion in 2026, according to Precedence Research in July 2026. This is close to the USD 10 trillion personal-transportation expenditure estimate cited by ARK-related research. It is the relevant long-run pool because autonomous vehicles could replace private ownership, taxis, ride-hailing and some public-transport journeys. Estimates for the labeled 2026 robotaxi market range from USD 1.187 billion at Grand View Research to USD 5.301 billion at SQ Magazine. This is not a forecast discrepancy to average: the smaller figures measure a new service category, while the larger figure measures activity the technology could eventually compete for. The option valuation uses the displaced-spend pool but assumes only 0.4% to 1.0% capture in successful cases. It does not capitalize a share of USD 9.98 trillion without margin and probability filters.
### The valuation requires measurable capture, not universal autonomy

The lower success case assumes USD 40 billion of annual network revenue, or 0.4% of USD 9.98 trillion, and USD 20 billion of EBITDA at a 50% margin. The higher case assumes USD 100 billion of revenue, a 1.0% share, and USD 50 billion of EBITDA. At an assumed realized fare of USD 0.50 per mile, these cases require 80 billion and 200 billion paid miles annually. At 60,000 paid miles per vehicle per year, they imply approximately 1.3 million and 3.3 million active vehicles. These are report estimates, not company guidance. They are far above the 42 Model Ys registered for driverless ride-sharing in Texas as of May 2026, showing the remaining fleet and permission challenge. The cases use 16.0x EBITDA in 2032 and success probabilities of 30% and 19%, leaving 51% as the zero-value failure outcome.
### Unit economics can work if utilization and safety coexist

Tesla targets a Cybercab operating cost near USD 0.20 per mile, versus AAA’s approximately USD 0.77 per mile cost to own and operate a new vehicle. At a USD 0.50 fare and USD 0.20 of direct operating cost, gross contribution before network overhead is USD 0.30 per mile, or 60%. At 60,000 paid miles per year, one vehicle would generate USD 30,000 of revenue and USD 18,000 of contribution. A USD 30,000 vehicle depreciated over five years adds USD 0.10 per mile at that utilization if it is not already included in the operating-cost target. This shows why cost definitions matter. Empty repositioning, cleaning, insurance, remote assistance and downtime could materially reduce margin. The option cases therefore assume a 50% EBITDA margin only at mature density, not during launch.
### Tesla has commercial momentum but limited comparable operating evidence

- Tesla reported robotaxi service in seven major US metropolitan areas by the end of Q2 2026 and targets roughly 12 states by year-end.
- Waymo reached 500,000 paid rides per week across ten US cities by March 2026 and about 15% of ride-hailing gross bookings in mature San Francisco and Los Angeles zones by June.
- Baidu Apollo Go completed 3.4 million fully driverless rides in Q4 2025 and reached 20 million cumulative rides by February 2026.
- Tesla’s Austin median wait time was reported at 15.32 minutes versus Uber’s 3.15 minutes, showing that availability and fleet density remain important.

Tesla’s operating-footprint claim is not the same as its regulatory permission. It can operate a branded robotaxi service under different permissions, safety-driver arrangements or geofenced conditions. Waymo’s 500,000 weekly paid rides and Baidu’s 3.4 million quarterly trips are clearer volume benchmarks than a city count. Tesla’s seven-metro expansion matters because it tests whether operations can be replicated, but Tesla has not disclosed active fleet size, rides, revenue, paid miles or remote-assistance frequency. The report therefore gives city expansion positive probability weight without treating it as proof of scaled driverless economics.
### Texas is permissive, while California remains the key US contrast

Texas granted Tesla Robotaxi LLC TNC permit 000143 for statewide automated operations from 6 August 2025 to 6 August 2026. Tesla self-certified its system as SAE Level 4 compliant under the new state framework. The evidence does not establish renewal after 6 August 2026, a material gap at the report date. In California, Tesla held only an Autonomous Vehicle Testing Permit with a driver as of 12 August 2026. It had neither a driverless testing permit nor a driverless deployment permit. Its Bay Area service used a standard TCP limousine permit, not CPUC authorization for commercial autonomous operation. Texas supports commercial testing, but this contrast prevents extrapolation to nationwide driverless permission.
### China and Europe add opportunity and liability gates

China’s GB 44721-2026 standard for Level 3 and Level 4 systems takes effect on 1 July 2027 and makes automakers liable for accidents within the operational design domain. Tesla was recruiting test technicians in nine Chinese cities and targeting broader regulatory progress during Q3 2026, but the register does not show comprehensive driverless commercial approval. In Europe, Dutch approval for FSD Supervised had been recognized by Lithuania, Estonia, Denmark and Belgium. This is a supervised-product milestone, not robotaxi approval. The UNECE WP.29 framework adopted in June 2026 may support mutual recognition across more than 60 countries, but national implementation and operational-design-domain approval remain necessary. The geographic picture is supervised use in selected European countries, testing and localization in China, permissive automated operation in Texas, and no driverless permission in California.
### Safety evidence is extensive for supervised driving, but limited for rider-only driving

Tesla owners have accumulated more than eight billion miles using FSD Supervised, a meaningful training-data asset. Tesla reported one major collision per 6.36 million Autopilot-engaged miles in Q3 2025. Another Tesla-derived dataset reported one major collision per 5.30 million FSD Supervised miles over a later twelve-month period. The figures cover different products or periods, so the report does not treat either as universally superior. Neither is directly comparable with rider-only operations because supervision changes intervention behavior and the risk population. Tesla defines its unsupervised threshold as approximately ten times safer than a human, but the public record lacks a driverless safety filing that lets investors test this by road type, weather and operating domain.
### Conflicting driverless-mileage estimates support an evidence discount

Public estimates differ sharply. Electrek reported approximately 380,000 cumulative driverless miles by mid-August 2026. A Medium operational summary cited nearly 700,000 cumulative paid robotaxi miles through February 2026, while another comparison cited roughly 1.7 million Tesla driverless miles by early 2026. These cannot all use the same definition and period. The report uses the lowest clearly described driverless figure and treats all estimates as unaudited because the sources do not reconcile paid miles, testing miles, safety-driver presence or remote assistance. Waymo, by comparison, had accumulated more than 170.7 million rider-only miles. Community tracking also placed Tesla FSD 12.6 at roughly 213 highway miles per disengagement, versus 9,793 miles per disengagement in Waymo’s 2024 California filing. Product, geography and reporting methods differ. The gap supports a high failure probability, not a conclusion that Tesla cannot close it.
### Hardware economics help, but legacy-fleet compatibility is a constraint

A Tesla vision-only sensor suite is estimated at approximately USD 400 per vehicle, compared with roughly USD 12,000 for a multi-sensor suite including LiDAR. If vision-only performance is sufficient, the hardware savings matter across millions of vehicles and support low-cost fleet deployment. However, Elon Musk confirmed that Hardware 3 vehicles cannot support unsupervised full self-driving and require Hardware 4 or later for future driverless use. This limits autonomous eligibility across part of the installed base and may create retrofit, customer-remedy and reputational costs. A consumer fraud class action alleging deceptive marketing of Hardware 1 through 3 as autonomy-capable remains unresolved. The model values consumer FSD separately and does not assume every paid FSD customer becomes a robotaxi supplier.
### Competition proves demand but raises the execution bar

Waymo’s mature-zone share shows that riders will use driverless services when wait times and coverage are competitive. Baidu demonstrates high trip volume under China’s operating framework. Uber provides a network-density benchmark and had a 14.1% forecast EBIT margin for 2026 in the peer pack, although it is asset-light and not a direct margin comparator for vehicle-owning robotaxis. Tesla’s vertical integration could retain vehicle-manufacturing margin, software margin and network take rate. It would also bear fleet depreciation, insurance and regulatory liability. North America’s reported share of the 2025 robotaxi market ranges from 54.09% to 90.0%; the difference reflects immature market definitions, so neither figure is used in valuation. The option instead uses explicit assumptions for revenue, margin and vehicle requirements.
### Probability weighting is the core valuation judgment

The lower case’s 30% probability reflects operation across seven reported metros, Texas authorization, a large supervised dataset and plausible cost architecture. The higher case’s 19% probability reflects the additional possibility that Tesla scales to more than one million vehicles and captures 1.0% of displaced transportation spending by 2032. The 51% failure remainder exceeds either success case because California driverless permission is absent, Texas permit renewal is unproven, comparable rider-only mileage remains limited and remote-intervention frequency is undisclosed. Failure does not mean FSD lacks consumer value; that value is captured in paid software. It means the separate driverless network does not reach the modeled scale and EBITDA within the valuation horizon.
### What would break the option upward or downward

The option rises if Tesla publishes auditable rider-only miles and interventions, secures driverless deployment approval in California, renews Texas authority, and demonstrates wait times and paid utilization approaching incumbent ride-hailing. A path toward 1.3 million active vehicles, realized pricing near USD 0.50 per mile and mature EBITDA margin near 50% would validate the lower case. The option falls if operations continue to depend on safety drivers or opaque remote assistance, if liability rules prevent economic insurance, or if Hardware 4 fails adverse-weather validation. A cost of USD 0.35 rather than USD 0.20 per mile would halve contribution at a USD 0.50 fare, from USD 0.30 to USD 0.15 before overhead. The division could win demand yet disappoint valuation if permission, safety or utilization prevents high-margin scale.

valuePools.name: Energy storage and solar
deepDive: ### The prize is avoided power cost and outage loss, not equipment revenue alone

The global battery-energy-storage market is projected to reach USD 96.8 billion in 2026 by BloombergNEF and Wood Mackenzie research published in March 2026. The economic pool is broader because storage and solar can replace fuel purchases, peak-generation capacity, grid upgrades and outage losses. SolarPower Europe estimated that solar could displace EUR 67.5 billion of EU natural-gas imports during 2026 if gas prices remained high. Oak Ridge National Laboratory put the cost of major US power outages at USD 121 billion in 2024. These regional figures cannot be combined into a clean global total because their geography and cost categories are inconsistent. The valuation therefore uses Tesla’s demonstrated revenue and gross profit rather than a global avoided-cost headline. Market growth supports volume, but battery inputs and project pricing determine the value Tesla retains.
### The required share is moderate relative to the labeled market

The base valuation applies 10.0x to the report’s target-year USD 7.0 billion EBITDA estimate, producing USD 70 billion of enterprise value. At a 25% EBITDA margin, this requires approximately USD 28 billion of annual revenue. That equals 28.9% of the USD 96.8 billion labeled 2026 BESS market if the market does not grow. This overstates the required future share because the target year is later than 2026 and the division also includes residential batteries, solar and services. Compared with FY2025 revenue of USD 12.771 billion, USD 28 billion requires a little more than doubling. The assumption is demanding but based on an existing profitable business, not a pre-revenue option. It depends on deployment growth without gross margins reverting toward lower-margin integrator levels.
### The disclosed segment is already economically material

Tesla’s verified Energy generation and storage segment produced USD 12.8 billion of external sales and USD 3.8 billion of gross profit in FY2025. It represented 13.5% of group revenue but 22.2% of group gross profit. Its implied gross margin is 29.8%, calculated as USD 3.8 billion divided by USD 12.8 billion. This compares favorably with the group’s 18.0% gross margin, calculated from USD 17.1 billion of gross profit and USD 94.8 billion of revenue. Tesla reports segment gross profit, not segment EBIT or EBITDA, so the report does not relabel gross profit as operating profit. The USD 7.0 billion target EBITDA is a modeled mature outcome that requires operating expenses to grow more slowly than revenue.
### Market position is strong but no longer first globally

- Benchmark Mineral Intelligence estimated BYD at 13% of the global BESS integrator market in 2025, ahead of Tesla.
- Tesla held an estimated 10% share in 2025, making it the second-largest global BESS integrator.
- Wood Mackenzie placed Sungrow at 9%, close enough that execution and regional mix can change the ranking.
- CATL held 27.1% of global ESS battery-cell shipments in H1 2026, showing meaningful upstream supplier power.

BYD’s first-place position matters because it combines vehicle and battery scale with aggressive pricing. Tesla’s second-place position still supports procurement leverage, project credibility and a global installed base, but market structure does not protect its position. Sungrow’s 9% share shows that the top three are closely grouped. CATL’s 27.1% cell-shipment share is a different market layer and should not be compared directly with integrator shares. It instead shows the concentration of a key input. Tesla can reduce supplier dependence through cell manufacturing and standardized Megapack design, but the evidence does not quantify the division’s internally sourced cell share.
### Lower cell costs expand demand but could be competed away

Stationary lithium-ion battery-pack prices fell to a record USD 70 per kWh in 2025, according to BloombergNEF. Lower input costs can improve project returns, support more deployments and widen Tesla’s gross margin if customer prices adjust with a lag. They can also lower system prices as BYD, Sungrow and other integrators pass savings to customers. The division’s 29.8% FY2025 gross margin shows Tesla retained meaningful value during falling battery costs, but one year does not establish through-cycle sustainability. A ten-dollar pack-cost movement across one gigawatt-hour equals USD 10 million of input economics before hedging, chemistry, balance-of-system costs and contractual pass-throughs. At scale, small cost-per-kWh changes matter more than modest shifts in solar-unit volume.
### Residential storage has brand strength, but source definitions differ

AgentSolar AI estimated that Tesla represented 65% of US residential solar-battery installation quotes in 2026, with Enphase second at 16.6%. Wood Mackenzie separately estimated Tesla reached 33.4% of US residential solar installations in Q4 2025. These are not conflicting measures of one market: the first covers battery quotes, while the second covers residential solar installations. Neither establishes Tesla’s global residential share. Together, they indicate a strong US consumer-energy position across Powerwall and solar. The valuation does not extend the 65% quote share globally because quotes may not convert to installations and no comparable global company ranking was found.
### Consumer pricing shows why installation economics matter

Powerwall 3 installed cost was estimated at USD 689 to USD 1,277 per kWh in 2026, far above the USD 70 per kWh stationary-pack benchmark. The difference includes the inverter, enclosure, software, installation labor, permitting, channel margin and warranty. Consumer-scale equipment also cannot be compared directly with bulk cells. This gap shows where value can be created or lost. At the low end, an installer can offer an attractive resilience product while retaining margin. At the high end, demand depends heavily on electricity tariffs, incentives and outage concerns. Tesla’s direct brand and integrated solar-plus-storage offer can reduce customer-acquisition and integration friction, but local permitting and installation capacity remain outside factory control.
### Utility storage and residential products carry different risks

Megapack-style utility projects provide large volumes, standardized hardware and potentially efficient factories, but customer concentration and contract timing can make quarterly revenue volatile. Powerwall has smaller tickets and a broader customer base, but adds installation, channel and regional-policy complexity. Solar can support storage sales but has historically been less differentiated than battery controls and grid services. The disclosed segment combines all three, so its 29.8% gross margin does not identify the source of incremental profit. The base case assumes storage remains the growth and margin engine, while solar supports customer acquisition rather than valuation. A shift toward low-margin project hardware would reduce EBITDA even if deployment rises.
### Manufacturing scale and battery allocation drive capacity economics

Tesla announced a USD 250 million Berlin investment supporting 18 GWh of annual 4680 cell production. At a USD 70 per kWh stationary-pack reference, 18 GWh equals USD 1.26 billion of cell value before yield, chemistry and end-use allocation. This is report arithmetic, not disclosed energy revenue. The same cells can supply vehicles or stationary storage, creating flexibility but also internal competition for capacity. If vehicle demand weakens, energy storage can absorb battery capacity and improve factory utilization. If robotaxi or vehicle demand rises sharply, internal allocation could limit Megapack growth unless cell capacity expands in parallel. Shared battery procurement is beneficial only if transfer pricing and capital allocation preserve division economics.
### The margin bridge to USD 7 billion EBITDA is visible

FY2025 revenue was USD 12.771 billion and gross margin was 29.8%, producing USD 3.802 billion of gross profit. If revenue reaches USD 28 billion and gross margin remains 29.8%, gross profit would be approximately USD 8.34 billion. A USD 7.0 billion EBITDA outcome would then leave only about USD 1.34 billion for cash operating costs below gross profit. That is a very lean cost burden unless material expenses are allocated corporately or software and service mix improves. At a more conservative 25% EBITDA margin, USD 28 billion of revenue produces exactly USD 7.0 billion of EBITDA, but still requires gross margin near 30% and operating expenses near 5% of revenue. The report treats this as an upper-middle base assumption, not a certainty. At a 20% EBITDA margin, USD 28 billion of revenue yields USD 5.6 billion and value falls by USD 14 billion at 10.0x.
### Comparable valuation does not support a software multiple

Fluence is the most focused listed storage comparator, but its forecast earnings are negative and its 2026 EV/Sales multiple is 0.7x, making EV/EBITDA unusable. Tesla’s division is profitable, integrated with cell sourcing and exposed to consumer storage, so it merits more than a distressed integrator revenue multiple. A pure software multiple would ignore working capital, factories, cells, warranty and project execution. The selected 10.0x EBITDA is below Teradyne’s 24.1x 2026 EV/EBITDA and the broad peer median of 13.0x, but above mature automotive manufacturing levels. It rewards growth and disclosed gross profitability while requiring cash conversion, not merely deployment volume.
### What would validate or break the energy value

Validation requires revenue to more than double toward USD 28 billion while gross margin remains in the high twenties, storage deployments grow and cash conversion survives project working-capital swings. Continued top-three global integrator share, sustained Powerwall leadership and additional cell capacity would support this outcome. The value falls if the USD 70 per kWh cell environment triggers an integrator price war, if CATL or BYD captures most upstream economics, or if project mix pushes gross margin below 20%. At USD 28 billion of revenue, a 20% EBITDA margin and 8.0x multiple produce USD 44.8 billion of enterprise value, 36% below the USD 70 billion base. Conversely, USD 35 billion of revenue at a 28% EBITDA margin and 12.0x produces USD 117.6 billion. Manufacturing scale matters only if Tesla retains battery-cost savings and converts deployment into durable gross profit.

valuePools.name: Paid driver-assistance and connected software
deepDive: ### The prize is recurring software revenue from mobility spending

Two MarketsandMarkets releases estimate the 2026 software-defined-vehicle market at USD 447.55 billion and USD 633.85 billion, a discrepancy too large to overlook. The report uses neither figure because both include hardware, architecture and services beyond Tesla’s paid subscriptions. The useful opportunity is the share of Tesla’s eligible fleet willing to pay for driver assistance, connectivity and upgrades. At 10 million cumulative vehicles produced by July 2026, every 10% of the fleet paying USD 99 per month would generate USD 1.19 billion of annual recurring revenue before churn and eligibility adjustments. The valuation requires USD 5 billion of target-year EBITDA, implying roughly USD 6.7 billion of revenue at a 75% EBITDA margin.
### Subscriber evidence supports a real profit engine

Tesla reached 1.48 million active FSD subscribers by Q2 2026, up 56% year over year, and reported a 55% subscription attach rate on new North American deliveries. At USD 99 per month, 1.48 million subscribers would imply USD 1.76 billion of gross annual billings if all paid the full price for twelve months. Third-party estimates of USD 66 million of monthly revenue, or USD 792 million annualized, imply an effective monthly yield of only about USD 44.60 per subscriber. The gap may reflect trials, legacy purchases, regional pricing, non-paying activations or differing definitions. The report therefore models FY2025 software revenue of USD 1.648 billion, comprising a USD 792 million recurring run-rate and approximately USD 856 million of annualized deferred FSD revenue recognition, twice the disclosed USD 428 million recognized in H1 2025.
### Deferred revenue improves visibility but complicates division boundaries

The FSD deferred-revenue balance was USD 3.87 billion at 31 December 2025. Recognition depends on feature delivery and accounting judgments, not simply subscription cash collection, so deferred release is not the same as recurring subscription revenue. Automotive sales revenue of USD 65.821 billion includes recognized FSD Supervised software, while connectivity may sit within broader service pools. Tesla does not separately disclose Premium Connectivity revenue. The modelled division therefore combines identifiable subscription economics and deferred recognition, then removes the same amount from automotive. This is a valuation boundary, not a company-reported segment.
### Competitive pricing limits unlimited revenue per user

- Tesla charges USD 99 per month after ending the USD 8,000 outright purchase option for new North American vehicles in February 2026.
- Ford reduced BlueCruise to USD 49.99 per month or USD 495 annually, with a USD 2,495 lifetime option.
- Mercedes priced Drive Pilot at USD 2,500 annually but paused rollout in January 2026 because of development cost and limited demand.
- Huawei reduced its Qiankun ADS advanced package to CNY 15,000 after subsidies from July 2026.

Ford had 1.22 million BlueCruise-equipped vehicles globally. GM had approximately 750,000 Super Cruise-enabled vehicles across 23 North American models and expected 850,000 active subscribers by year-end 2026. These installed-unit figures are not directly comparable with Tesla’s active subscribers, but they show paid assistance is becoming competitive rather than proprietary. GM software services reportedly retain about 70 cents of every revenue dollar, supporting the report’s 75% mature EBITDA assumption as ambitious but possible. Tesla benefits from an integrated fleet and rapid over-the-air updates. Its disadvantage is that the product promise is tied to unsupervised autonomy expectations and legacy-hardware limits.
### Value depends on retention, not one-quarter attachment

A 55% North American attachment rate matters only if subscribers remain after trials and through product cycles. Reaching USD 6.7 billion of revenue at USD 99 per month requires approximately 5.64 million full-price subscriber-equivalents, calculated as USD 6.7 billion divided by USD 1,188 annually. At the estimated effective yield of USD 44.60 monthly, the same revenue requires approximately 12.5 million subscribers. The base case therefore assumes subscriber growth, higher effective yield, connectivity and deferred recognition, not simply extrapolation of the current count. Hardware 3’s inability to support unsupervised driving may increase cancellations or legal remedies, but supervised features can retain value independently. The division merits 15.0x EBITDA, above automotive but below valuations assuming sustained hypergrowth.
### What would validate or break the software value

Validation requires active subscribers to exceed five million, effective revenue per subscriber to move toward the USD 99 list price, and retention to remain strong after the shift to subscription-only sales. Continued 50%-plus attachment would expand the installed base, while transparent recurring revenue and gross margin would reduce the boundary discount. The value falls if the 1.48 million figure includes many non-paying or discounted users, if Hardware 3 remedies consume deferred revenue, or if Ford and GM force lasting price reductions. At USD 50 of effective monthly revenue and five million subscribers, annual revenue is only USD 3.0 billion. At a 75% margin and 15.0x, value would be USD 33.8 billion. This downside shows why paid attachment and retention, rather than the global SDV market label, determine valuation.

valuePools.name: Optimus general-purpose robotics
deepDive: ### The prize is manual-labor spending, not today’s humanoid market

Humanoid robots could eventually compete for annual manual-labor spending measured in trillions of dollars. One broad industry analysis places the theoretical labor-displacement opportunity at USD 60 trillion. That is a ceiling, not an investable market, because much human work cannot be automated economically or legally within the forecast horizon. The labeled 2025 humanoid market is also disputed: Fortune Business Insights estimated USD 4.89 billion, while Grand View Research estimated USD 2.4 billion. Forecasts for 2035 range from USD 15 billion at Interact Analysis to USD 38 billion at Goldman Sachs. The valuation uses neither total labor spending nor the labeled market without a volume bridge. It models future EBITDA from industrial deployment and applies explicit success probabilities.
### The option requires industrial scale, not household ubiquity

The lower success case assumes USD 8 billion of EBITDA in 2033, while the higher case assumes USD 25 billion. At a 30% EBITDA margin, these outcomes require approximately USD 26.7 billion and USD 83.3 billion of revenue. At an average USD 25,000 selling price, they imply roughly 1.1 million and 3.3 million annual unit-equivalents before service revenue. These volumes are far beyond current evidence and require automotive-style production, a global integrator ecosystem and repeat purchases. The report assigns a 25% probability to the lower case and 14% to the higher case, leaving a 61% zero-value failure outcome. The failure probability reflects technology, production, safety and customer-integration gates, not a lack of labor demand.
### Current operational evidence is narrow but relevant

Tesla has confirmed three autonomous factory tasks: sorting 4680 battery cells, moving parts between stations and visual quality inspection. These tasks are useful because Tesla controls the factory environment, process design and training-data loop. They do not prove general-purpose operation, because repetitive cell sorting and parts movement can be engineered around a robot. Gen 3 reportedly has 22 degrees of freedom per hand and 50 total actuators, up from 11 hand degrees of freedom in Gen 2, expanding manipulation potential. The target payload is 20 kilograms in dynamic carry and approximately 68 kilograms in a deadlift. Missing evidence includes task cycle time, intervention frequency and mean time between failures, all necessary for labor-cost comparison.
### Production claims conflict, so the official update carries more weight

One secondary report claimed mass production began on 21 January 2026 and exceeded 1,000 units by mid-year. Other estimates put internal deployment above 1,000 units, while a separate external estimate suggested fewer than 100. Tesla’s Q2 2026 update said output remained effectively zero because first-generation lines were still being installed, with production expected later in the year. The report uses the official statement and treats higher counts as prototypes, development units, misclassification or unverified reporting. This distinction matters economically: a training fleet is not saleable output, and unit count without utilization does not establish revenue capacity. Fremont’s former Model S/X line is being converted for Optimus production, demonstrating capital commitment but not production yield.
### Labor economics can be powerful if reliability is high

Loaded annual labor cost for a US manufacturing worker was estimated at USD 95,000 to USD 156,000, while Optimus operating-cost estimates ranged from USD 2 to USD 10 per hour. A robot operating 20 hours per day would provide 7,300 hours annually, equal to approximately 3.5 standard 2,080-hour shifts. At USD 10 per hour, operating expense would be USD 73,000 before depreciation, maintenance, supervision and integration. Adding a USD 25,000 purchase price depreciated over five years takes this to USD 78,000, potentially below one loaded worker and far below three shifts. At the estimated current manufacturing cost of USD 50,000 to USD 100,000, depreciation and support could remove that advantage. Utilization and autonomy matter more than the purchase-price target.
### Tesla’s target price is not yet its estimated cost

Tesla targets an at-scale selling price of USD 20,000 to USD 30,000, while current R&D-phase manufacturing cost is estimated at USD 50,000 to USD 100,000 per unit. Reaching the target requires at least a 40% cost reduction from the low end and up to 80% from the high end merely to sell at USD 30,000 without a gross loss. Unitree’s G1 is available to developers from approximately USD 16,000, showing that a low sticker price is not unique, although capability and industrial durability differ. Agility’s Digit is offered at approximately USD 8,500 per month, or USD 102,000 annualized, under a service model that bundles support and uptime. Tesla must compete on productive output per dollar, not hardware price alone.
### Competitors offer more auditable deployment benchmarks

- AgiBot held 44% of global humanoid shipments in H1 2026, while Unitree held 31%.
- China-based manufacturers represented an estimated 97% of H1 2026 humanoid shipments, while North America held 43.4% of 2025 market revenue under a different market definition.
- Figure 02 logged 1,250 runtime hours and moved 90,000 parts at BMW between November 2025 and June 2026.
- Agility Digit moved more than 100,000 totes in a live GXO Logistics deployment.

The 97% shipment share and 43.4% North American revenue share are not contradictory because one measures units in H1 2026 and the other measures revenue in 2025. They indicate that Chinese vendors dominate lower-cost volume, while North American firms command higher development valuations and contract revenue. Figure’s documented runtime and parts movement provide the operating evidence Tesla has not disclosed. Agility’s tote milestone likewise shows a narrow but live commercial workflow. Tesla’s advantages are manufacturing scale and internal demand; externally verifiable deployment evidence remains thinner. Option probability should rise only when productive hours, failure rates and customer economics become comparable.
### General-purpose capability must overcome integration friction

Sixty-one percent of surveyed industrial organizations identified integration with existing systems as a primary barrier to humanoid adoption. A robot must connect with warehouse software, safety systems, tooling, charging, maintenance and production scheduling. Tesla can simplify internal integration by redesigning its own processes, but external customers may not adapt factories around Optimus without proven savings. The July 2026 acquisition of a Virtuix Omni One Enterprise teleoperation system indicates use of human-controlled data generation. That is rational during training, but it also shows autonomy is incomplete. Teleoperation can resolve edge cases, yet frequent remote assistance changes the labor-displacement economics. The key measure is autonomous productive minutes per paid support minute, which Tesla does not disclose.
### Safety and regulation create a separate commercial gate

A reported near-miss involved an Optimus unit dropping a battery module in a restricted Fremont area, although no major human injury incidents were reported in commercial humanoid deployments through early 2026. One event does not establish an unacceptable safety rate, but it shows the consequences of heavy mobile machines operating near people. EU Regulation 2023/1230 and ISO 10218:2025 become central to CE-marked robot compliance from 20 January 2027. The EU AI Act also classifies autonomous humanoid robots as high-risk systems, with full compliance required for European access from August 2027. These rules require risk assessment, safeguards, documentation and monitoring. A robot that operates only behind fences may still be valuable, but its task range and general-purpose claim would be narrower.
### The valuation multiple recognizes industrial quality and option risk

The option cases use 18.0x EBITDA, below Teradyne’s 24.1x 2026 EV/EBITDA and Fanuc’s 29.0x, but above conventional manufacturing. These listed companies have positive, diversified automation revenue and established service organizations, while Optimus is pre-revenue. Probability weighting, rather than an artificially low multiple, captures most pre-commercial risk. Figure AI’s reported USD 39 billion private valuation shows investor willingness to value humanoid potential, but private funding valuation is not a substitute for unit economics. Discounting future EBITDA from 2033 also recognizes the time needed to build production and customer deployment. This produces material option value without assuming Tesla captures the labor market.
### What would validate or break the robotics option

Validation requires saleable output, several thousand externally deployed units, documented productive hours and reliable completion of multiple tasks without continuous teleoperation. Cost must fall below USD 30,000 while price remains sufficient for positive gross margin, and customers must show payback against loaded labor and integration costs. A useful intermediate gate would be 7,300 annual operating hours at more than 90% scheduled uptime, with disclosed interventions and safety incidents. The option falls if Tesla can automate only three tightly engineered factory tasks, if current USD 50,000 to USD 100,000 cost persists, or if integration requires dedicated human supervision. At a USD 50,000 price and only 100,000 annual units, revenue would be USD 5 billion, far below the USD 26.7 billion lower success case. The key evidence is economically useful multi-task reliability, not staged dexterity demonstrations.

valuePools.name: Supercharging network
deepDive: ### The prize is a share of road-fuel spending

The global EV-charging-station market was estimated at USD 22.93 billion in 2026 and projected to grow at 25.37% annually through 2034 by Safe Electric in July 2026. Road fuel is the incumbent expenditure pool, but estimates of the 2026 gasoline market vary sharply: Grand View Research put it near USD 1.8 trillion, while Process Integration estimated USD 140.36 billion. The definitions clearly differ by geography, product scope or value-chain stage, so the report does not average them. Charging valuation uses connectors, energy throughput and tariff evidence rather than a share of gasoline spending. Tesla needs only a small share of transport-energy spending, but it must earn that share after electricity, rent, maintenance, payment and capital costs.
### Throughput per connector is the decisive bridge

Tesla’s network reached an estimated 82,357 connectors by Q2 2026, and average daily throughput exceeded 268 kWh per stall in Q3 2025. Together, these figures imply approximately 22.1 GWh per day and 8.06 TWh per year if connector count and throughput are simultaneously representative. At USD 0.43 per kWh, gross customer billings would be USD 3.47 billion. At USD 0.35 per kWh, they would be USD 2.82 billion. This supports the independent USD 3.6 billion FY2025 paid-charging revenue estimate as plausible, though it is not company-reported. It also shows why normalized throughput matters more than station count. A low-utilization connector can expand coverage while reducing near-term returns.
### The revenue boundary is modelled from a disclosed pool

Tesla reported USD 12.530 billion of FY2025 Services and Other revenue, including paid Supercharging, used vehicles, maintenance, collision repair and insurance. The report assigns USD 3.600 billion to paid charging using the cited annual run-rate estimate and retains approximately USD 8.930 billion of residual services in automotive. Free Supercharging costs are allocated to Automotive cost of revenue, while paid sessions sit in Services and Other cost of revenue, making gross-margin reconstruction difficult. The report models USD 720 million of current gross profit at a 20% margin and does not present it as reported profit. This avoids assigning zero revenue to a functioning network or double counting with automotive.
### Utilization evidence supports attractive mature sites

North American Superchargers reached a peak of ten sessions per stall per day in 2025. If the average session delivers 26.8 kWh, ten sessions exactly reconcile to 268 kWh of daily throughput. This is report arithmetic and indicates that the two utilization disclosures are economically consistent. At USD 0.43 per kWh, a stall would generate approximately USD 115 of daily revenue and USD 42,100 annually. At USD 0.35 per kWh, annual revenue would be approximately USD 34,200. These are averages before idle fees and membership economics. Site-level outcomes will vary widely because highway, urban, destination and new locations ramp differently.
### Capital cost differs sharply by ownership model

Tesla’s internal V4 infrastructure cost was projected below USD 40,000 per stall, while Supercharger for Business quoted USD 940,000 all-in for a standard eight-stall site. The latter equals USD 117,500 per stall and includes hardware and installation for a third-party host, so it is not directly comparable with Tesla’s internal equipment cost. At USD 42,100 of annual revenue per stall, simple revenue payback is under one year on USD 40,000 of infrastructure and 2.8 years on USD 117,500, before electricity and operating costs. At a 30% gross contribution margin, capital payback extends to approximately 3.2 years and 9.3 years, respectively. This makes site selection and host economics as important as manufacturing cost.
### Opening the network expands demand and increases service obligations

SAE finalized J3400, based on Tesla’s North American Charging Standard, in September 2024. Standardization reduces integration friction for other vehicle brands and could make Tesla’s network a default fast-charging venue. More compatible vehicles can increase paid throughput, particularly where Tesla has superior density and reliability. They also create congestion risk for Tesla owners and require adapter, payment and vehicle-software integration. Value rises if non-Tesla traffic fills off-peak capacity without requiring disproportionate investment. It falls if peak congestion requires costly capacity that remains underused outside travel periods.
### The business program adds a capital-light fee layer

Tesla charges businesses using Supercharger for Business USD 0.10 per kWh for software, billing and network operations. At 268 kWh per stall per day, this generates approximately USD 9,782 of annual platform revenue per stall. Across an eight-stall site, this is about USD 78,300 annually before equipment economics. The model can create a capital-light network layer when a host funds the USD 940,000 site, although the host must earn an acceptable return after electricity and Tesla’s fee. The platform opportunity should earn more than owned energy resale, but it remains too small and early to value separately. The base multiple reflects a blend of owned infrastructure and platform economics.
### Competition is measurable, but the requested global share ranking is incomplete

- Electrify America held an estimated 7.9% of US DC fast-charging ports in mid-2026.
- ChargePoint held an estimated 6.9% of US DC fast-charging ports over the same period.
- Tesla had 82,357 estimated global connectors, but the register did not provide a directly comparable US port-share percentage.
- J3400 standardization strengthens Tesla’s connector position without ensuring pricing power.

The missing Tesla US share prevents a clean ranked market-share table with a single denominator. Connector count is also an imperfect measure because charging speed, uptime, location and throughput vary. Electrify America is a direct highway fast-charging competitor, while ChargePoint’s broader model includes host-owned hardware and software. Tesla combines owned-network economics, support for vehicle sales and third-party platform fees. This integration creates strategic value but complicates standalone profitability. The valuation therefore relies on throughput and EBITDA rather than an unsupported market-share premium.
### The route to USD 2 billion of EBITDA is demanding but measurable

The base bridge uses USD 2.0 billion of target-year EBITDA and 12.0x, producing USD 24 billion of enterprise value. At a 30% EBITDA margin, revenue must reach USD 6.67 billion. At USD 0.40 per kWh, this requires 16.7 TWh of annual paid energy, approximately double the 8.06 TWh run-rate derived from current connectors and throughput. Tesla could achieve this by doubling connectors at unchanged throughput, doubling throughput on the existing base, raising price, adding business-platform fees, or combining these levers. A more realistic mix, 120,000 connectors at 320 kWh daily and USD 0.40 per kWh, would produce about USD 5.61 billion of energy billings before ancillary fees. The balance would require platform, access or higher tariff revenue.
### Margin depends on the electricity spread

At a USD 0.40 retail tariff and assumed all-in electricity cost of USD 0.20 per kWh, the energy gross spread is USD 0.20, or 50%, before site rent, maintenance, network operations and depreciation. If electricity cost rises to USD 0.28 without tariff recovery, spread falls to USD 0.12, or 30%. After overhead and depreciation, EBITDA margin could fall from roughly 30% to the mid-teens. Tesla does not disclose national average electricity procurement cost or charging net margin, so these are report assumptions. Dynamic pricing can protect returns but may reduce customer preference where competing networks are available. The key variable is normalized paid energy throughput multiplied by net spread, not the headline tariff.
### Strategic value should not be double counted

Supercharging supports vehicle demand by reducing range anxiety and may improve Tesla retention even when sessions are free or low margin. That strategic benefit partly belongs in automotive pricing and volume, while paid-session cash flow belongs here. The report values only modeled charging EBITDA and adds no separate brand or ecosystem premium. Free-charging costs remain in automotive COGS, consistent with the disclosed accounting boundary. Opening the network to non-Tesla vehicles may reduce exclusivity but improve standalone utilization. The division can therefore become more valuable financially even as its vehicle moat narrows.
### What would validate or break the charging value

Validation requires annual energy throughput to approach 17 TWh, connector utilization to remain at or above 268 kWh per day as the network grows, and EBITDA margin to reach approximately 30%. Host-funded deployment with USD 0.10 per-kWh platform fees would improve capital efficiency. The value falls if new sites dilute utilization, electricity costs cannot be passed through, or competitors secure the best locations. At USD 6.67 billion of revenue and an 18% margin, EBITDA would be USD 1.2 billion and value USD 14.4 billion at 12.0x, 40% below base. Conversely, 20 TWh at USD 0.42 per kWh produces USD 8.4 billion of billings; a 35% margin and 14.0x would support USD 41.2 billion. The network is valuable, but current disclosure does not support treating it as a toll road with guaranteed utilization.

Energy and vehicles compete for cells but benefit from shared procurement and power electronics. Charging supports automotive demand, but only paid-session economics are valued in charging; free-session costs remain in automotive.

Automotive cash flow funds robotaxi and Optimus before either option is self-financing. Fremont’s Model S/X line conversion shows that optionality can consume current capacity and capital rather than arriving at no cost.

The followed forecast produces USD 12.4 billion of 2026 EBITDA and USD 3.5 billion of FCFF. The market-implied DCF instead requires USD 36.6 billion of EBITDA in 2026 and USD 61.4 billion in 2027 despite declining revenue.

The reverse case takes EBIT margin from 33.1% to 59.4% in one year and ultimately to 64.0%. That requires software and autonomous networks to dominate while the current revenue base remains manufacturing-heavy.
The SOTP target assigns material value to robotaxi and Optimus. The disagreement is over timing and probability, not whether the options exist.
scenarios: The bear scenario assumes continued automotive pricing pressure, normalized energy margins, lower charging utilization and no commercially meaningful EBITDA from either pre-revenue option. Revenue is approximately USD 90 billion and EBITDA USD 8 billion, with option legs effectively zero.

The base scenario assumes automotive recovery through utilization, more than doubling energy revenue while retaining strong gross profitability, expanding software subscriber-equivalents, and roughly doubling charging energy throughput. Robotaxi and Optimus contribute probability-weighted option values, not consolidated near-term revenue.

The bull scenario assumes California and other strict jurisdictions permit scalable driverless operations, Tesla approaches its robotaxi cost target, Optimus achieves reliable external deployment, and profit engines fund expansion without balance-sheet stress. Revenue rises to USD 250 billion and EBITDA to USD 100 billion, with materially stronger cash accumulation than in the base case.
coreAnalysis.bottomLine: Tesla owns several assets that could reinforce one another, but the share price assumes favorable interaction before key safety, permission, margin and production gates are independently proven. The USD 161.7 target is not automotive-only: it includes substantial software, energy, charging, robotaxi and robotics value. The SELL call reflects the fact that the current market capitalization requires success probabilities and group margins not yet supported by operating evidence.

risks.prose:
The main risk is correlation. Weak automotive pricing would be manageable if software, energy and autonomy generated cash. Heavy option investment would be manageable if manufacturing margins were strong. The damaging outcome is simultaneous automotive compression, elevated capital expenditure and delayed permission.

Several risks can be tracked before reported revenue changes. Driverless permit status, rider-only interventions, energy gross margin, charging throughput and Optimus productive uptime are direct leading indicators. Investors should not treat subscriber counts, city counts, connector counts or prototype demonstrations as substitutes for the economic measures those counts are intended to produce.

valuation.methodRationale:
SOTP is necessary because automotive, software, charging and energy have different margins and capital intensity, while robotaxi and Optimus are pre-revenue options. Profit engines use target EBITDA multiples inside relevant manufacturing, mobility and automation brackets; options use future EBITDA, explicit success probabilities and discounted scale years.

The target is the probability-weighted parts sum. A group EV/EBITDA sensitivity is shown only as an equivalent cross-check: it demonstrates how quickly value changes when aggregate EBITDA or the capitalization rate moves, but it does not replace the division bridge.

What the market is pricing.

The current USD 1,295.8bn EV exceeds the report’s USD 409bn undiscounted profit-engine value by about USD 886.8bn. Using the same discounted option scale values, the quote requires roughly 95% combined weighted success across the robotaxi and Optimus high-value legs, versus approximately 88 percentage points of stated leg probability in the base bridge and substantial failure remainders. It effectively prices broad success rather than optionality.

The market assumes Rapid transition to software-like group margins, including 59.4% EBIT margin in 2027. We assign a different reading: The followed model reaches 8.1%; automotive margin and capex evidence do not support the market-implied transition speed. (Tesla Q2 2026 update and MLQ.ai, July–August 2026: 16.3% automotive gross margin ex-credits and $5.8bn quarterly capex.)

The market assumes Driverless permission and safety scale are close to nationwide replication. We assign a different reading: Texas supports a positive option, but California’s with-driver-only status and limited comparable rider-only evidence require a majority failure allowance. (California DMV, 12 August 2026; Waymo comparison, 21 April 2026.)

The market assumes Optimus can move directly from prototypes to high-volume, positive-margin production. We assign a different reading: Official near-zero output, $50,000–100,000 estimated cost and missing reliability metrics justify probability weighting rather than a mature robotics value. (Tesla Q2 2026 update, 22 July 2026; Optimus cost estimate, June 2026.)
